The study used three different Savonius rotor wind turbine models with varying blade sizes: Model 1 (height 1 m, diameter 0.4 m), Model 2 (height 0.75 m, diameter 0.3 m), and Model 3 (height 0.5 m, diameter 0.2 m).
A constant wind speed of 9.2 m/s was used in the simulations.
The simulations were carried out using a transient time flow with a constant upstream wind speed.
The SIMPLE algorithm was used for the pressure-velocity coupling scheme in the solution method.
The power coefficient of all models increased with tip-speed ratio (TSR), and the highest efficiency was obtained at almost a unity (0.9) TSR.
Model 2 generated the highest power coefficient, followed by Model 3 and Model 1.
The torque and torque coefficient were higher at low TSR and decreased as the TSR increased for all models.
Model 3 showed an enhanced performance percentage of 38.54% and 27.87% in power and power coefficient at TSR of 0.7 and 0.9, respectively, compared to the baseline.
Model 2 had an improvement of 39.08% and 28.10% in power and power coefficient at TSR of 0.7 and 0.9, respectively, compared to the baseline.
The difference in peak power coefficient between the best performing model (Model 2) and the worst performing model (Model 1) was 25.62%.
The starting capability of the wind turbine, which could be affected by the blade size, was not covered in the current study.
The performance of the Savonius rotor wind turbine was influenced by factors such as blade angle, blade shape, and the lift and drag forces acting on the blades.
The primary goal of the study was to maximize wind energy harvesting and rotational mechanical electric generation of Savonius rotors by varying the rotor blade size.
The Savonius wind turbine is a vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) that is propelled by drag and has strong starting torque and no wind direction issues.
Compared to horizontal-axis wind turbines (HAWTs), VAWTs like the Savonius rotor receive less attention, and their design research is sparse and unreliable.
